To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“NGO researchers working at a distance can create new knowledge through their local collaborators, but this is often a process that reinforces the power dynamics of the Global North and the Global South.”
the use of local brokers in the production of knowledge in Tajikistan has both positive and negative effects on knowledge production and that there are ways to mitigate these negative effects.

The use of long-distance research methods in NGO work in Tajikistan is problematic, but can be made less so by paying attention to the power dynamics and ownership of the research process and by working with the local brokers to develop a shared understanding of the research aims and methods.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which international NGOs’ long-distance research practices can be both emancipatory and neo-colonial.
the ways in which NGOs are reﬂecting upon their own knowledge production and how this is changing.
how NGOs can work with local partners in ways that are more collaborative, less extractive, more respectful, and more accountable to local needs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the long-distance research approach has both beneﬁts and pitfalls, and that it is not a panacea.

long-distance approaches to research in international development are not inherently good or bad, but rather the way in which these methods are used can have a variety of consequences for the production of knowledge.
the long-distance approach to knowledge production is a double-edged sword.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the process is a complex, messy one, but one that is worth pursuing, as the alternative is to do nothing, and to leave people in a position where they cannot speak for themselves.
, in the case of NGOs, distance can be a productive space for the development of knowledge, but it can also reproduce the coloniality of power.
, while we have been able to produce some knowledge through our long-distance research, we have also had to confront some of our own assumptions and biases in the process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ‘distance’ of knowledge production is not a given, but rather something that needs to be actively negotiated, with the potential to be either empowering or disempowering for local actors.

the Global North–Global South divide is not a binary one, but rather one that needs to be understood as a spectrum, and that the power relations between the North and the South are not uni-directional.
the Global South has a lot to teach the Global North, if only we would listen.
